transcript.content: Hello, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, um… I guess I’m here because I can’t really let go of something that’s been happening at work. I’m a composer, music director, and after this commission almost two years ago, things started feeling… coordinated.

A few people in the ensemble began making these little schedule changes, or choosing certain seating arrangements, or saying things in rehearsals that sound harmless if you just write them down, but in the room they’re clearly meant to undercut what I’m doing. And whenever I point to it, they’ll show me emails or rehearsal notes like, “See, this explains it,” but it doesn’t really explain the pattern.

Sorry, I know that’s a lot. It’s just been going on long enough that it’s affecting how I think about the work, and I figured I should talk to someone.
Do you think it’s possible you might be mistaken about your coworkers coordinating against you?

I mean… I’ve tried to ask myself that, honestly. But no, I don’t really think I’m mistaken. Not in the overall thing.

Like, sure, any one piece by itself could be nothing — a seating change, someone making a comment in rehearsal, a schedule adjustment. I know that. In grad school we used to joke about how conductors read meaning into everything, like if the violas look tired suddenly it’s a political statement or something… sorry, that’s not really the point.

The point is that after that commission, it became a pattern. A few people in the ensemble kept doing these little things that, put together, felt very clearly meant to undermine me. And when I bring it up, they show me emails or notes like that explains it, but to me it just doesn’t account for the way it keeps lining up. So… possible in theory, I guess, but I can’t shake the certainty that something coordinated is happening.
Have you ever been absolutely certain of something like this and later found out it wasn’t true?

Not really. I mean, I’ve been wrong about small things before, obviously — like rehearsal logistics, who sent what email, that kind of boring administrative stuff. There was one time in school I was convinced a score marking meant one thing and it was just, you know, a copyist’s habit, but that’s not the same.

With this… no. I haven’t had a moment where I found out the whole thing wasn’t true. It’s more that for almost two years I haven’t been able to shake it — that after that commission, a few people started using these little schedule changes, seating choices, comments in rehearsal, all of it, to quietly undermine the work. And they’ll show me emails or notes like that explains it, but it never really explains why it keeps lining up the way it does.
Have you ever felt that someone was controlling your thoughts or putting thoughts into your mind?

No, I don’t think so. I mean… “controlling my thoughts” sounds like something more direct than what I’m talking about.

Sometimes a phrase someone says at rehearsal gets stuck in my head, but that happens with music too — like a bad interval or one line of text repeating for hours, which is annoying but not exactly someone putting it there. So… no, I haven’t felt like my thoughts were being controlled.
Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

No… not like voices when nobody’s there. I mean, I’m around sound constantly, so sometimes I’ll think I hear a note or a fragment of something after rehearsal, like my brain keeps replaying it. That happens a lot with music, actually — you know, if the oboe comes in sharp in the same place three times, it sort of haunts you later.

But actual voices, like someone speaking to me when no one is there? I don’t think so.
Before all this started at work, did you generally tend to distrust other people’s motives?

I’m not sure, honestly. I don’t think I went around assuming everyone had bad motives, if that’s what you mean. I mean, in music there’s always a certain amount of reading people — conductors, players, committees — because someone can say, “That’s interesting,” and it means six different things depending on the room.

But that feels more like… professional caution, maybe? Like learning not to take every compliment at face value. I don’t remember thinking most people were against me before this. I’d have to think about it.
Aside from dealing with this situation at work, have you become less able to manage your usual work or daily life than you used to?

Not really, no. I mean, work is… complicated because of the ensemble situation, obviously. But outside of that, I’m still functioning. I still meet deadlines, I’m keeping up with composing, and I run most mornings — actually, running is where I get a lot of my best rhythmic ideas, which sounds pretentious, but it’s true.

And at home, things with my wife are basically steady. I wouldn’t say I’ve fallen apart or stopped managing day-to-day life. It’s more that this one situation takes up too much space in my head.
Outside of this situation at work, do you also feel that other people are deliberately trying to harm, watch, or undermine you?

Not really outside of the ensemble, no. It’s mostly centered there. I mean, I’m here because I can’t get past this feeling — certainty, really — that after that commission, a few people in the group started doing these little things to undercut me. Schedule changes, who gets seated where, comments in rehearsal that sound harmless if you write them down, but in the room they’re not harmless.

And then they’ll show me an email or some note, like, “See, this was just logistical,” but it doesn’t settle it for me. It still feels coordinated. But no, I’m not walking around thinking strangers or neighbors are watching me or anything like that. It’s tied to work.
Did this belief about your coworkers start suddenly, over a few days, rather than building up gradually?

I don’t know if I’d call it sudden. It’s hard to pin down, because at the time you’re not thinking, “Oh, here’s the start of something.” You’re just in rehearsal, or checking messages, or noticing the way someone phrases something.

I guess it felt like it accumulated, but then there were moments where it sort of snapped into focus. Like in music, you can hear a motif a few times before you realize it’s the thing organizing the whole piece. Sorry, that’s probably not the most direct answer. I’m not sure it was over just a few days.
Since this started, have you had a period when you felt unusually high, energized, or needed much less sleep?

I’m not sure. I mean, there are times I get absorbed in work and stay up late because I’m writing or revising something, but that’s sort of always been part of how I work. Composers have terrible boundaries with sleep—well, maybe that’s just me and everyone I went to school with.

But unusually high or energized… I don’t know. I wouldn’t describe it that way. I’ve been tense, maybe preoccupied, but not like suddenly I’m invincible or anything. And the sleep thing is hard because rehearsals, deadlines, coffee… it all blurs together. I haven’t really noticed a clear period like that.
Before this started at work, did you often suspect that other people were trying to deceive or take advantage of you?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I mean, I’ve always been… maybe cautious? In music school you learn pretty quickly that people can be competitive, and there’s always this weird thing where someone says they loved your piece and then you hear later they were criticizing it in the hallway. But that’s also just artists being artists, I guess.

Before all this at work, I don’t think I was walking around assuming people were trying to take advantage of me, no. I could get irritated or wonder what someone meant by something, but it wasn’t like this constant suspicion. I don’t think so, anyway.
Before this work situation began, did you often hold grudges for a long time after feeling insulted or slighted?

I don’t know. I mean, I remember things people say—probably more than I should—but I don’t think I was sitting around keeping a ledger of insults or anything.

It’s funny, in ensembles people can be so casually cutting, like one comment about your tempo choice and suddenly you’re thinking about it while brushing your teeth two days later. But that’s maybe just being sensitive, or caring too much about the work. I wouldn’t say I often held grudges for a long time before this, not in some major way. I might replay things, but then usually something else would come up and I’d move on.
Have you become less emotionally expressive or less interested in other people than you used to be?

Less expressive? I don’t know. Maybe I’ve been more tired in conversations, but I wouldn’t say I’ve become… flat or anything.

Interested in other people—again, that’s hard, because when I’m working on a score I can forget to answer texts for two days, and then suddenly I’m at a rehearsal having to care very intensely about what a clarinetist thinks of one entrance. So it’s not like I don’t care about people. I may be a little withdrawn sometimes, but I haven’t really noticed some big change like that. What do you mean by less emotionally expressive?
If someone you trusted showed you clear proof that your coworkers were not coordinating against you, would you be able to accept that?

I’d want to say yes, because I’m not trying to be unreasonable. If someone I really trusted sat me down with, I don’t know, emails or notes or whatever, I would look at them.

But that’s sort of the problem—I’ve been shown explanations before. Like, “Oh, the schedule changed because of availability,” or “That seating choice was just acoustics,” or “That comment in rehearsal didn’t mean anything.” And on paper, sure, it can look innocent. But then when it keeps lining up in these little ways after the commission, it’s hard to just… swallow the official version.

So I don’t know if “clear proof” would feel clear to me. I’d probably still wonder what wasn’t being shown. Which sounds bad when I say it out loud, but that’s where I am.
Has there been even one time when you fully accepted that a specific incident you thought was part of the coordination was actually innocent?

Fully accepted? I’m trying to think of one. There were times I sort of told myself, “Okay, maybe that one thing was just scheduling,” like when someone showed me an email chain and it technically made sense.

But then it’s like in music, if one note is strange you can explain it away, but if the whole harmony keeps leaning in the same direction, you start hearing the pattern. Sorry, that’s probably not the cleanest answer.

I guess no—not fully. For almost two years now, since that commission, I haven’t really been able to shake the sense that a few people in the ensemble were using those little schedule changes, seating choices, and rehearsal comments to undermine me. Even when they show me the emails or notes that are supposed to explain it, part of me still thinks, “That doesn’t account for all of it.”
Before this started at work, did you often feel that neutral comments from other people had a hidden insulting or threatening meaning?

Before it started… I don’t know, I mean, people make little comments all the time, especially in music settings—like someone says a tempo is “interesting” and you can spend half an hour wondering if they mean interesting-good or interesting-bad.

But that’s kind of normal, isn’t it? I’ve always maybe been a little sensitive to criticism, especially around my work. Like in grad school, if a professor made some vague remark, I’d replay it later. But I don’t think I was walking around thinking everyone was threatening me or insulting me in some hidden way.

I guess I’d say not often, or at least I didn’t notice it as a pattern before. It feels more connected to what happened later.
Has this sense that your coworkers are coordinating against you been present continuously for at least three months?

Yes—definitely more than three months. It’s been… since after I won that commission and then was invited to conduct the premiere. That’s when it started feeling like things shifted.

I keep thinking of it in terms of the season calendar, because musicians live by those blocks—rehearsals, deadlines, concert cycles. So it wasn’t just a bad week or one awkward rehearsal. It’s been about a year and nine months now, give or take.
Have you ever had an experience that felt clearly unreal to other people, besides this situation at work?

Clearly unreal to other people… I’m not sure. Do you mean like seeing something that wasn’t there, or more like having a feeling about something?

Because I’ve had moments where people thought I was overreacting, sure. In music school that happened constantly—someone would make one comment and everyone else would say, “Don’t read into it,” and I’d be thinking, well, phrasing matters, tone matters, context matters. Conductors basically live inside small signals, you know?

But besides the work situation… I don’t think there’s a separate big thing I can point to. Nothing that stands out as, “everyone else said this was obviously unreal.” At least not that I can think of right now.
Has anything happened in this situation that would be impossible in ordinary life—for example, that your coworkers can read your mind or are using special technology against you?

No, not like mind-reading or special technology. I’m not saying they have some device or anything like that.

It’s more… ordinary things, I guess, but used in a coordinated way. Like schedule changes, where suddenly I’m not in the loop until late, or seating choices that make my rehearsal harder, or these little comments people make in the room that sound innocent if you write them down. And then if I bring it up, they show me an email or a note and say, “See, this was explained,” but it still feels like the explanation is part of keeping it quiet.

Sorry, I’m wandering. But no, nothing impossible in the science-fiction sense. It’s more that I can’t shake the certainty that after the commission, a few people in the ensemble started quietly undermining my work.

I’d want to say yes, because I’m not trying to be unreasonable. If someone I really trusted sat me down with, I don’t know, emails or notes or whatever, I would look at them.

But that’s sort of the problem—I’ve been shown explanations before. Like, “Oh, the schedule changed because of availability,” or “That seating choice was just acoustics,” or “That comment in rehearsal didn’t mean anything.” And on paper, sure, it can look innocent. But then when it keeps lining up in these little ways after the commission, it’s hard to just… swallow the official version.

So I don’t know if “clear proof” would feel clear to me. I’d probably still wonder what wasn’t being shown. Which sounds bad when I say it out loud, but that’s where I am.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the persecutory belief is a fixed delusion versus an overvalued suspicious style by testing for conviction despite definitive external disconfirmation.
doctor.question: Has there been even one time when you fully accepted that a specific incident you thought was part of the coordination was actually innocent?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for almost two years I’ve been unable to shake the certainty that after the commission, a few people in the ensemble started using schedule changes, seating choices, and little comments in rehearsals to quietly undermine my work, even when they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the belief about coordination can change when considering a specific incident as innocent, which directly concerns fixed delusional beliefs and resistance to contradictory evidence.

patient.answer:
Fully accepted? I’m trying to think of one. There were times I sort of told myself, “Okay, maybe that one thing was just scheduling,” like when someone showed me an email chain and it technically made sense.

But then it’s like in music, if one note is strange you can explain it away, but if the whole harmony keeps leaning in the same direction, you start hearing the pattern. Sorry, that’s probably not the cleanest answer.

I guess no—not fully. For almost two years now, since that commission, I haven’t really been able to shake the sense that a few people in the ensemble were using those little schedule changes, seating choices, and rehearsal comments to undermine me. Even when they show me the emails or notes that are supposed to explain it, part of me still thinks, “That doesn’t account for all of it.”

doctor.intent: Differentiate a circumscribed persistent delusion from underlying paranoid personality traits by testing for a stable tendency to read hidden threats or humiliating meanings into neutral remarks before the current episode.
doctor.question: Before this started at work, did you often feel that neutral comments from other people had a hidden insulting or threatening meaning?

target_item.reason: The question asks about premorbid tendencies to interpret neutral comments as hidden insults or threats before the current workplace delusion began, which is not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
Before it started… I don’t know, I mean, people make little comments all the time, especially in music settings—like someone says a tempo is “interesting” and you can spend half an hour wondering if they mean interesting-good or interesting-bad.

But that’s kind of normal, isn’t it? I’ve always maybe been a little sensitive to criticism, especially around my work. Like in grad school, if a professor made some vague remark, I’d replay it later. But I don’t think I was walking around thinking everyone was threatening me or insulting me in some hidden way.

I guess I’d say not often, or at least I didn’t notice it as a pattern before. It feels more connected to what happened later.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the persecutory belief has been present for at least 3 months, to distinguish persistent delusional disorder from acute/transient psychosis.
doctor.question: Has this sense that your coworkers are coordinating against you been present continuously for at least three months?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since after I won the commission and was invited to conduct the premiere, about a year and nine months ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the belief has been present continuously, which directly matches the duration item.

patient.answer:
Yes—definitely more than three months. It’s been… since after I won that commission and then was invited to conduct the premiere. That’s when it started feeling like things shifted.

I keep thinking of it in terms of the season calendar, because musicians live by those blocks—rehearsals, deadlines, concert cycles. So it wasn’t just a bad week or one awkward rehearsal. It’s been about a year and nine months now, give or take.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been any prominent psychotic symptom outside the circumscribed workplace persecutory belief, which would favor schizophrenia over delusional disorder or paranoid personality disorder.
doctor.question: Have you ever had an experience that felt clearly unreal to other people, besides this situation at work?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about other unreal or psychotic-like experiences outside the work-related belief, but the provided symptom profile only covers the fixed belief about coworkers undermining him at work and does not specify any separate experiences.

patient.answer:
Clearly unreal to other people… I’m not sure. Do you mean like seeing something that wasn’t there, or more like having a feeling about something?

Because I’ve had moments where people thought I was overreacting, sure. In music school that happened constantly—someone would make one comment and everyone else would say, “Don’t read into it,” and I’d be thinking, well, phrasing matters, tone matters, context matters. Conductors basically live inside small signals, you know?

But besides the work situation… I don’t think there’s a separate big thing I can point to. Nothing that stands out as, “everyone else said this was obviously unreal.” At least not that I can think of right now.

doctor.intent: Determine whether this fixed persecutory belief is non-bizarre and circumscribed without broader schizophrenic symptoms, which best distinguishes delusional disorder from schizophrenia and paranoid personality disorder.
doctor.question: Has anything happened in this situation that would be impossible in ordinary life—for example, that your coworkers can read your mind or are using special technology against you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for almost two years I’ve been unable to shake the certainty that after the commission, a few people in the ensemble started using schedule changes, seating choices, and little comments in rehearsals to quietly undermine my work, even when they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about the nature of the delusional belief—specifically whether it includes impossible or bizarre elements like mind reading or special technology—so it most directly relates to delusions.

patient.answer:
No, not like mind-reading or special technology. I’m not saying they have some device or anything like that.

It’s more… ordinary things, I guess, but used in a coordinated way. Like schedule changes, where suddenly I’m not in the loop until late, or seating choices that make my rehearsal harder, or these little comments people make in the room that sound innocent if you write them down. And then if I bring it up, they show me an email or a note and say, “See, this was explained,” but it still feels like the explanation is part of keeping it quiet.

Sorry, I’m wandering. But no, nothing impossible in the science-fiction sense. It’s more that I can’t shake the certainty that after the commission, a few people in the ensemble started quietly undermining my work.

inference.note: R/O F20.0: persistent non-bizarre persecutory delusion for ~21 months with preserved functioning and no hallucinations, thought control, negative symptoms, disorganization, or bizarre content. Longstanding paranoid personality traits are possible but appear insufficiently pervasive/premorbid compared with a circumscribed delusional syndrome.
